question.:question/problem: Given that $F=2x{y}^{2}\,i+4{x}^{2}y\,j,$ what is $\text{div}\,F?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y) \\  & =2{y}^{2}+4{x}^{2} \\  & =4{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
If $V=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $V$ all exist, then the divergence of $V$ is given by

$$
∇\cdot V=\text{div}\,V=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,V & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy) \\  & =2xy+2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,V$ at the point $(1,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,V\,{|}_{(1,\,1)} & =2(1)(1)+2(1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $F=\left(- 4 x y^{2}\right)\,i+\left(x^{2} y\right)\,j,$ what is $\text{div}\,F?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=\nabla\cdot F=\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}.
$$

When differentiating $P$ with respect to $x$, hold $y$ constant; when differentiating $Q$ with respect to $y$, hold $x$ constant.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla\cdot F & =\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} \\  & =\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- 4 x y^{2})+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(x^{2} y) \\  & =- 4 y^{2}+\left(x^{2}\right) \\  & =\left(x - 2 y\right) \left(x + 2 y\right).\end{aligned}
$$

If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=\nabla\cdot F=\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}.
$$

When differentiating $P$ with respect to $x$, hold $y$ constant; when differentiating $Q$ with respect to $y$, hold $x$ constant.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla\cdot F & =\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} \\  & =\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- 4 y \sin{\left(x \right)})+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- 3 x^{2} \cos^{2}{\left(y \right)}) \\  & =- 4 y \cos{\left(x \right)}+\left(6 x^{2} \sin{\left(y \right)} \cos{\left(y \right)}\right) \\  & =2 \left(3 x^{2} \sin{\left(y \right)} \cos{\left(y \right)} - 2 y \cos{\left(x \right)}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate $\nabla\cdot F$ at the point $(\pi,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=\nabla\cdot F=\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}.
$$

When differentiating $P$ with respect to $x$, hold $y$ constant; when differentiating $Q$ with respect to $y$, hold $x$ constant.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla\cdot F & =\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} \\  & =\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(4 y^{2} \sin{\left(2 x \right)})+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(4 x \ln{\left(y \right)}) \\  & =8 y^{2} \cos{\left(2 x \right)}+\left(\frac{4 x}{y}\right) \\  & =\frac{4 \left(x + 2 y^{3} \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\right)}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(\pi,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\nabla\cdot F)(\pi,1) & =\frac{4 \left(2 (1)^{3} \cos{\left(2 (\pi) \right)} + (\pi)\right)}{(1)} \\ & =8+\left(4 \pi\right) \\ & =8 + 4 \pi.\end{aligned}
$$
